fixes.explanation: Grief is a real feeling, friend, but it's not in this verse. Solomon says wrath is cruel and anger is like a flood, "…but who can withstand jealousy?" I think he saved the toughest question for last. I'd rather face a hot oven than that question.

Gentle sounds right, but it isn't the word the verse uses. It reads, "The wounds of a friend are faithful, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful." A kiss can feel gentle and still be deceitful, so how it feels doesn't tell you much. The verse is about whether you can trust it.

Weary is a fair guess, but the verse names a different soul. It says, "The soul that is full loathes honey, but to a hungry soul, any bitter thing is sweet." Full versus hungry is the whole contrast, and weary isn't in the picture. I think a hungry baker would take a broken cookie corner and call it a feast.

A ship is a nice picture, but it isn't in the verse. The text says, "Like a bird that strays from its nest is a man who wanders from his home." So the comparison is a bird and a nest. No harbor, no sails, just a bird that strays from its nest.

The verse doesn't say prophet, friend. It says, "…the counsel of a friend is sweetness to the soul." Oil and incense bring joy to the heart, and the verse sets a friend's advice right beside them. I'd hand a prophet a cookie anyway, but this verse only names a friend.
True. The verse says, "better a neighbor nearby than a brother far away." Solomon puts the one nearby ahead of the one far away. I'd say that's a good reason to be kind to whoever lives next door.

It's actually true, friend. The verse says, "better a neighbor nearby than a brother far away." Solomon ranks the two, and the neighbor nearby comes out on top. Nearby wins over far away in this line.

False is right. The verse says, "The prudent see danger and take cover, but the simple keep going and pay the penalty." The prudent are the ones who see danger and take cover. The simple keep going and pay. I've smelled smoke from an oven and gone to open a window, and I recommend it.

His garment is right. The verse says, "Take the garment of him who posts security for a stranger…" That's Solomon's advice about a man who has posted security for a stranger. The verse names a garment, nothing fancier. Nice and plain, like a good cookie recipe.

A sandal is close, but the verse says garment. It reads, "Take the garment of him who posts security for a stranger…" The man has posted security for a stranger, and Solomon's advice is to take his garment. The sandal didn't make the cut. My own handle has a name carved on it, but that's a different story.

A gift is a nice thought, but that's not the word. The verse says the loud morning blessing "…will be counted to him as a curse." The blessing is loud and early, and the verse says it counts as a curse. Volume and timing matter more than I'd have guessed.

Sharpens is the word. The verse says, "As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another." Iron does the sharpening to iron, and one man does it to another. I spent years soft around the edges, so I know who I'd like next to me.
Testing shows up in verse 21 of this chapter, but not here. This verse says, "As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another." The verb is sharpens, iron on iron and one man on another.

Honored fits the second blank. The verse says the one who looks after his master "…will be honored." Just like tending the tree gets you the fruit, looking after your master gets you honor. Care leads to a reward in both halves.

Crushed away for good sounds hopeful, friend, but the verse says otherwise. It reads, "Though you grind a fool like grain with mortar and a pestle, yet his folly will not depart from him." Grinding is rough treatment, and the folly still stays. I've pressed plenty of dough, and some things just don't flatten out.
